opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I've played with it a fair amount, mostly on things I care about: math reasoning, some coding, and research-style questions where you have to keep a long chain of thought consistent.

My overall impression is that it's a solid step forward, though not a discontinuous jump like R1 was. R1 surprised everyone because it showed that RL with verifiable rewards could get you strong reasoning cheaply, and it came out open. V4 feels more like an engineering consolidation. The reasoning is more stable, it rambles less, and it handles long context better. On coding it's quite usable now. For many everyday tasks I wouldn't feel a big gap versus the top closed models.

Where I still see weaknesses is in really open-ended research problems. If you give it something without a clear answer, where you have to propose a new direction, judge whether an idea is actually interesting, or notice that the question itself is wrong, it still tends to follow familiar patterns. It produces something that looks reasonable but isn't deep. That's true of basically all current models, not just DeepSeek. Benchmarks don't capture it well, because benchmarks by definition have answers.

What I find most interesting about DeepSeek is less any single model and more their approach. They're very focused on efficiency: architecture choices, training cost, inference cost. They keep showing that you don't necessarily need the biggest cluster to stay near the frontier if you think carefully about the whole stack. For the field, especially the open-source community, that's very healthy. It pushes everyone to ask whether scale is the real bottleneck or whether we've been inefficient.

So my short answer is that it's very good, cost-effective, and a strong open option. The bigger question it raises for me is what comes after this phase. Once everyone converges on similar recipes, the differentiation has to come from somewhere else, probably from better understanding why these models work, not just training them bigger.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I'll say up front that my view is based on hands-on use rather than any inside knowledge, and I try to be careful not to over-read a few weeks of prompting.

The honest summary is: it's a very strong model, and the thing that impresses me most isn't any single benchmark number, it's the consistency on the kind of tasks I actually care about. I spend a lot of time on reasoning, search, and planning problems, so my first instinct with any new model is to throw hard math and algorithmic problems at it, things where the answer isn't memorizable and you have to actually hold a chain of argument together. On those, V4 holds up well. It doesn't just produce a plausible-sounding derivation, it tends to notice when a step doesn't follow and backtrack, which is the behavior you want to see. A year or two ago that was rare; now it's table stakes for a frontier model, and V4 clears that bar.

On coding, it's genuinely useful. I use it for the boring but error-prone stuff, refactoring research code, writing a training loop with the right sharding, debugging a stray shape mismatch. It's good at reading a messy codebase and inferring intent. Where it still stumbles is the long-horizon part: if I give it a task that takes many steps and the state has to be tracked over a long interaction, it can drift, lose a constraint I gave earlier, or confidently "fix" something that wasn't broken. That's not unique to DeepSeek, every model I've used has some version of this, but it's where I'd still want a human in the loop.

What I find most interesting as a researcher is the efficiency story. The capability per dollar, both in training and in inference, is the real headline. They've continued down the path of being very deliberate about architecture and systems co-design, and you can feel it in how cheap it is to run at scale. That matters for people like me, because it changes what experiments are affordable. It also puts pressure on the rest of the field to be honest about how much of the frontier is really about compute versus smart engineering.

Where I'd be more skeptical: I don't think I can judge things like robustness, safety behavior, or performance in languages and domains I don't work in, from personal use alone. And I always discount my own impressions a bit, because the problems I pick are biased toward what I find interesting. So my overall take is: it's clearly at or near the frontier on reasoning and code, the efficiency is the thing to pay attention to, and the open questions are the same open questions everyone has, long-horizon reliability and agentic use in the wild.

r001.rationale: The response discusses consistency and long-horizon drift, but does not say DeepSeek V4 becomes more capable after an initial warm-up with substantial context.
